words.lemma: gonaid (3pl. negative imperative/jussive after ná: 'let them not slay')

cognate: OIr. gonaid : Ved. han- (*gʷʰen-); OIr. bó, acc. boin : Ved. gáv-/gó-, acc. gā́m (*gʷṓws, acc. *gʷṓm); cf. Av. jan- + gāuš
drift_or_renewal: none in the verb-object pair; Irish also has the action noun guin bó and the compound epithet Bó-guine, Vedic the compound gohán- 'cow-slayer' and the privative cow-name aghnyā́- ('not to be slain', *n̥-gʷʰn-)
shared_syntax: verb *gʷʰen- with *gʷōw- as direct object (Irish negative jussive 'let them not slay the cow'; Vedic conditional 'if you slay our cow')
context: In both, slaying a cow is a wrong that brings ruin on the slayer. Irish (Expulsion of the Déssi, both versions): a druid goes in the form of a hornless red cow to be killed by the enemy, so that the killers are defeated; the enemy's druid orders 'let the men not slay the cow', the horse-boys slay it, and he cries woe. The Dindshenchas of Tailtiu lists guin bó m-blicht ('slaying of milch cows') among three forbidden crimes, and Bó-guine is a stigmatising epithet glossed 'slaying of the cows'. Vedic AVŚ 1.16.4 (= AVP 1.10.4) curses the demon who slays 'our cow, horse, man'; in the Brahmagavī hymns the cow, being slain, destroys the slayers (AVŚ 5.18.11) and is addressed as aghnyā́; RV 7.56.17 prays that the Maruts' cow-slaying, man-slaying weapon be far off; Gathic Y 32.14 condemns those who order the cow to be slain. The verb and the noun are the ordinary words for 'slay' and 'cow' in Irish and Indic, so the bare pair is close to predictable. What lifts it above chance is the matching frame: a prohibition on, or ruin following, the slaying of the cow, which appears in three separate Irish texts and across Vedic and Avestan. The Dindshenchas list is Christianised (it is ascribed to Patrick), and the Indo-Iranian side is a cultic notion (aghnyā́) rather than one fixed line.
phrase: *gʷʰen- *gʷōm 'slay the cow' (as a tabooed, ruinous act): OIr. ná gonat ... in boin / guin bó ~ Ved. gā́m han- / gohán- / aghnyā́ ~ Av. gāuš jaidiiāi

note: All 152 bundles read in order. Almost all partners are late Greek prose (GLAUx), Menota, Notker or other prose, matched on common roots. One low claim: gonaid + bó ~ han- + gā́m, 'slaying the cow' as a tabooed act (BC-a2bc7). Leads rejected: BC-5e40c, bodar/badhirá with *ḱlew- 'hear' (contexts not congruent: an Irish riddle vs. a Vedic image); BC-e780f, Irish list 'cow, man, ox, horse' (generic list of property, and no Vedic partner in that bundle); BC-cd8f2, fír flathemon (its only cross-branch partner is a mis-mapping of ON vár 'spring'); BC-a7500/BC-20e84 and others, no shared wording.
